historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Penicillins

starting.description: On an accidentally mould-contaminated staphylococcal culture plate, nearby bacteria were observed undergoing lysis. Fleming subcultured the mould and developed its diffusible antibacterial activity into the named penicillin culture filtrate, which he studied for bacterial selection and possible treatment.

inspiration.description: A mould-produced diffusible antibacterial substance and the observed lysis of staphylococci near its colony.

steps.description: Fleming noticed bacterial lysis around a contaminating mould and investigated the resulting antibacterial mould-culture filtrate.
Fleming demonstrated selective use in bacteriological cultures and suggested possible therapeutic application.
Oxford researchers developed injectable penicillin as systemic chemotherapy and demonstrated activity in mice, stimulating subsequent clinical use, according to Rolinson's retrospective.
The phenoxymethylpenicillin branch provided an acid-stable oral penicillin. A 1988 institutional report describes production by mould fermentation with a phenoxyacetic acid precursor.

Fermentation and assay work yielded 6-APA, the nucleus to which new side chains could be attached. Semisynthetic branches sought wider activity, oral absorption, or penicillinase stability; these include amoxicillin and flucloxacillin.

design.description: Researchers cultivated the mould and developed an active filtrate, established systemic experimental treatment, used precursor-fed fermentation for penicillin V production, and recovered 6-APA for side-chain changes to improve absorption, broaden activity or improve stability against penicillinase.

circumstances.description: The plate contamination and associated lysis were unexpected observations during staphylococcal work; the mould subculture and examination of its diffusible activity were deliberate follow-up.

limits: The penicillin V production and acid-stability history is a retrospective summary, not a reading of its original preparation reports; Oxford's animal-treatment and clinical transition are supported by a participant retrospective, not the unread 1940 article.
conflicts: In the Wellcome witness transcript, Doyle and Rolinson differ about the timing and communication of the 6-APA assay discrepancy (S5, E13).

NTP and Batchelor describe penicillin V as prepared in 1948 (S3, E8; S5, E12), whereas a 1955 abstract states Brandl and colleagues produced it in 1953 (S6, E14). Batchelor dates recognition of its useful properties to 1954, while NTP cites a 1953 Brandl paper for low-pH activity. The exact priority and whether these descriptions refer to distinct events have not been adjudicated.
gaps: The 1940 Oxford primary report has been located but not yet read; the penicillin V original preparation and low-pH studies have not been read.
